As it's stated, your question seems to be asking others to do the work of understanding the topic and then breaking it down for you which is not really inline with the way discussions on this server work.... Eh, I think in the case of cryptography that is often necessary. There are *very* few people in the world who understand cryptography well enough to evaluate a novel concept, and it is unrealistic for everyone to go "learn cryptography". Okay then just - is it feasible? I don't fully understand witness encryption (just started reading up) but it looks really cool. Main concern I have is with how it handles difficulty adjustments Seems approximation / handwavey I generally agree with Piper's sentiment, as we do get a lot of such questions in this server, but I feel like that class of questions is appropriate beyond a certain minimum threshold of understanding where you really do need an expert that you probably can't find anywhere else. On the flip side, I can appreciate the desire to not have to draw a fuzzy line where "Is X possible?" is acceptable in some contexts but not others. Yeah, don't take my statement as a fundamental axiom I'm happy to summarise what I've understood of it so far but didn't want to in case I get it wrong feasible question is better. Without having read the paper my gut reaction based on what I know is to say, "no", I can't imagine how this would work, but that answer doesn't mean much because... I didn't read the paper 🤣 In this context does "unlocking" a file mean something like "decryption"? Haha makes sense. Witness encryption is broadly just - create a ciphertext that can be decrypted by only someone who has a solution to a hard problem (NP). And in this case that problem is blockchain Yup, finding out the key to decrypt the file The gist, as I understand it, is that you encrypt something with a key that is not yet known but will eventually be known. However, I'm quite confident the cryptography here is beyond me, it feels like it is in the realm of zkSNARK stuff (which is also beyond me). You are basically saying, "I want to encrypt this thing with the key that is returned by this function" where "this function" is something that hasn't been executed yet (and in this case, may take a very long time to execute). One can imagine a very weak similarity here to public key cryptography, where you are encrypting something with the public key. In that case, the public key is the returned value from "the function" so definitely not a perfect analogy, but we can see how one can imagine a system where you can encrypt something without knowing the decryption key. Nice summary, thank you! Also potentially a very wrong summary. Nope, it's correct This is summary for witness encryption Well, correct only if witness encryption is actually a real thing that one can do. 😄 I still classify witness encryption as black magic. Decryption key is found by someone who has solution to a hard problem. But you don't need to know this solution to encrypt Why Because it makes no sense to my brain how that can be possible. If I accept that witness encryption is a thing, the leap to using Bitcoin's hashing function as "the function" is actually quite easy for me. It is the first leap to witness encryption that I cannot grok. I will read more and see if I can understand how they do it then :) Witness encryption isn't invented by authors of this paper though No, but it is invented by other humans outside of my knowledge network. 😆 My knowledge network doesn't have a lot of cryptographer nodes, and I haven't heard of any of them talking about witness encryption. This doesn't mean it isn't real, only that if it is it exists outside of my knowledge network at the moment. Thus, it is black magic. 😄 This went above my head but does "this is being taught in UC Berkeley" count for legitimacy? No. UC Berkeley is not within my knowledge network. 🙂 For cryptography I'd rather trust "these cryptographers all consider each other reputable" than "I know this cryptographer well" cause I don't know how to evaluate a good or bad cryptographer :) Bad = good but makes mistakes, not bad sorry
